title: The lactate shuttle
goal: Explain how lactate moves from the cells that make it to the cells that burn it, which transporters carry it, and which part of the shuttle idea is still argued.

steps.title: From fast fibres to slow ones
steps.text:
George Brooks' [lactate shuttle](g:lactate-shuttle) idea turns lactate from waste into a delivery. Lactate made in one cell is exported, then burned or reused by another [[c:cellcell]]:

- inside one working muscle, from fast glycolytic [fibres](g:muscle-fibre) to the slow oxidative fibres next to them;
- from working muscle, through the blood, to the heart, brain, liver and kidneys.

Support for this cell–cell shuttle is now close to unanimous. It also changes how to picture metabolism: glycolysis and oxidation are not alternatives that take turns, but two linked halves. Lactate, the product of one, is the fuel of the other [[c:linked-pathways]].

claims.text: Lactate is exchanged between glycolytic and oxidative fibres within a muscle, and from working muscle to heart, brain, liver and kidneys; experimental support for the cell–cell shuttle is essentially unanimous.

evidence.quote: Examples of the cell-cell shuttles include lactate exchanges between between white-glycolytic and red-oxidative fibres within a working muscle bed, and between working skeletal muscle and heart, brain, liver and kidneys.

There is essentially unanimous experimental support for a cell-to-cell lactate shuttle, along with mounting evidence for astrocyte-neuron, lactate-alanine, peroxisomal and spermatogenic lactate shuttles.

claims.text: Glycolysis and oxidation are linked rather than alternative processes, because lactate from one is the substrate of the other.

evidence.quote: The presence of lactate shuttles gives rise to the realization that glycolytic and oxidative pathways should be viewed as linked, as opposed to alternative, processes, because lactate, the product of one pathway, is the substrate for the other.

steps.title: MCT1 and MCT4: the doors
steps.text:
Lactate doesn't slip freely through cell membranes. It crosses on [MCTs](g:mct) (monocarboxylate transporters), which carry each lactate together with an H⁺, so they also help control the fibre's pH [[c:mct-proton]]. Muscle has two main kinds [[c:mct-types]]:

| | MCT1 | MCT4 |
|---|---|---|
| found in | slow, oxidative fibres; heart | fast fibres |
| main job | lactate **in** | lactate **out** |
| affinity | high (Km about 3.5–5 mmol·L⁻¹) | low (Km about 17–34 mmol·L⁻¹) |

The low affinity suits MCT4: it works best when lactate inside a hard-working fast fibre is high. MCT1 picks lactate up even when blood levels are low. Much of this map comes from rat muscle.

claims.text: Lactate crosses the muscle membrane on proton-linked monocarboxylate transporters, which take part in muscle pH regulation.

evidence.quote: The stereoselective transport of L-lactic acid across the plasma membrane of muscle fibres has been shown to involve a proton-linked monocarboxylate transporter (MCT) similar to that described in erythrocytes and other cells.
This transporter plays an important role in the pH regulation of skeletal muscle.

claims.text: MCT1 is highest in oxidative fibres and mainly takes lactate up; MCT4 sits in fast fibres and mainly exports it; MCT4 has a much lower affinity (higher Km).

evidence.quote: Collectively, these data suggest that MCT1 and MCT4 are primarily responsible for lactate uptake from the circulation and lactate extrusion out of muscle, respectively.
The kinetic activities of MCT1(Km=3.5 mM) and MCT4 (Km= 17-34 mM) are quite different.
expression of MCT1 is highest in the more oxidative muscles and very low in white muscles that are almost entirely glycolytic

steps.title: A favourite fuel: heart, slow fibres, brain
steps.text:
Given the choice, many tissues pick lactate. In people, working skeletal muscle and the beating heart use lactate in preference to glucose and fatty acids, and the brain prefers it to glucose [[c:preferred-fuel]].

That matters in a hard session: when blood lactate is high, the heart takes up more and burns it, and the brain draws on it too. High blood lactate also turns down the use of glucose and fat elsewhere [[c:lactate-spares]]. So lactate is not just used up; it steers which fuels the body burns.

Lactate is easy to burn: LDH, running in reverse, turns it back into pyruvate in one step, ready for the mitochondria.

claims.text: In humans, working skeletal muscle and the heart prefer lactate over glucose and fatty acids as a fuel, and the brain prefers it over glucose.

evidence.quote: In functioning humans …, working human skeletal muscles …, as well as in the beating hearts of those individuals …, lactate is preferred over glucose and fatty acids as a fuel.
Lactate is preferred over glucose as a fuel in brain preparations … and, most importantly, in humans in vivo …

claims.text: High blood lactate down-regulates the use of glucose and free fatty acids.

evidence.quote: In vivo, lactate is a preferred substrate and high blood lactate levels down-regulate the use of glucose and free fatty acids (FFA).

steps.title: Inside the cell: a shuttle under debate
steps.text:
Brooks goes further, to an *intracellular* shuttle: lactate made in a fibre's cytosol enters that fibre's own mitochondria, is turned back into pyruvate there by an LDH attached to them, and is oxidised [[c:intracell-shuttle]].

Not everyone agrees. One group isolated mitochondria from human and mouse thigh muscle, found no LDH in them, and saw that they could not use lactate [[c:no-mito-ldh]]. A middle view: lactate is the main form in which pyruvate travels through the cytosol, and is turned back into pyruvate *next to* the mitochondria.

What is settled: lactate moves between cells and is burned. Where the last step happens inside the cell is still argued.

claims.text: Lactate formed in the cytosol is oxidised via a lactate oxidation complex in the mitochondria of the same cell.

evidence.quote: Lactate, which is always produced in cytosol of muscle and other tissues because of the abundance, activity, and characteristics of cytosolic LDH, is oxidized to pyruvate via the lactate oxidation complex in mitochondria of the same cell.
It was concluded that skeletal muscle mitochondria are devoid of LDH and unable to metabolize lactate.

claims.text: Mitochondria isolated from human and mouse vastus lateralis contained no LDH activity and did not respire on lactate.

evidence.quote: Lactate did not cause respiration, nor did it affect the respiration of pyruvate + malate.
It was concluded that skeletal muscle mitochondria are devoid of LDH and unable to metabolize lactate.

debate.question: Do muscle mitochondria take up and oxidise lactate directly?

sides.position: Yes: a lactate oxidation complex with LDH in the mitochondria lets them take up lactate and oxidise it (the intracellular lactate shuttle).
No: isolated muscle mitochondria contain no LDH and can't use lactate, so lactate must become pyruvate in the cytosol first.
In between: lactate is the main form in which pyruvate moves through the cytosol, and is converted back near the mitochondria.

points: Cell–cell shuttle (well supported): fast fibres export lactate; slow fibres, heart, brain, liver and kidneys take it up.
Glycolysis and oxidation are linked halves: lactate from one is the fuel of the other.
MCTs carry lactate with an H⁺: MCT4 (fast fibres, low affinity) mostly exports, MCT1 (oxidative fibres, heart, high affinity) mostly imports.
Heart, working muscle and brain prefer lactate as a fuel, and high lactate turns down glucose and fat use.
Whether mitochondria oxidise lactate directly (the intracellular shuttle) is still debated.

variants.stem: During a steady 2-hour ride, the fast fibres in a cyclist's thighs keep releasing lactate. Where does much of it go during the ride?

options.text: Into nearby slow fibres, the heart and other tissues, as fuel
options.why: Right: this is the cell–cell lactate shuttle; producer cells feed consumer cells.

options.text: It collects in the muscle until the ride is over
options.why: Lactate is exported on MCTs and used within minutes; it doesn't sit in the muscle for hours.

options.text: It is lost from the body in sweat and urine
options.why: Only a tiny share leaves this way; almost all is oxidised or turned into glucose.

options.text: It waits in the blood for the liver to clear it after the ride
options.why: Removal happens during exercise too, by working muscle, heart and liver at once.

variants.stem: In a 10 km run at steady pace, lactate leaves the runner's fast fibres. What happens to most of it during the run?

options.text: Slow fibres and the heart take it up and oxidise it
options.why: Right: lactate is shuttled from producer to consumer cells and burned.

options.text: It stays stored in the muscle until the run ends
options.why: Lactate is exported and used continuously; there is no store of it.

options.text: It is lost from the body in sweat
options.why: Sweat carries a tiny amount; the bulk is burned.

options.text: It is turned back into glycogen in the same fast fibres
options.why: Fast fibres mostly export lactate; most of it is oxidised elsewhere or made into glucose in the liver.

variants.stem: Why does Brooks call glycolysis and oxidation "linked, as opposed to alternative" pathways?

options.text: Lactate made by glycolysis in one place fuels oxidation in another
options.why: Right: the product of one pathway is the substrate for the other.

options.text: Both pathways need oxygen at every step
options.why: Glycolysis needs no oxygen; the link is lactate, not oxygen.

options.text: They take turns: glycolysis first, then oxidation
options.why: That is the 'alternatives' picture Brooks rejects; they run at the same time.

options.text: Both take place inside the mitochondria
options.why: Glycolysis runs in the cytosol; oxidation in the mitochondria.

variants.stem: Which transporter mainly moves lactate out of fast, glycolytic muscle fibres?

options.text: MCT4
options.why: Right: MCT4 sits in fast fibres and mainly exports lactate.

options.text: MCT1
options.why: MCT1 is highest in oxidative fibres and the heart, and mainly takes lactate up.

options.text: GLUT4
options.why: GLUT4 carries glucose into muscle, not lactate out.

options.text: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump
options.why: This pump moves sodium and potassium; lactate needs an MCT.

variants.stem: MCT4 has a low affinity for lactate (Km about 20 mmol·L⁻¹); MCT1 a high one (about 5 mmol·L⁻¹). Why does this suit their jobs?

options.text: MCT4 works best when fast fibres are full of lactate; MCT1 grabs lactate even at low levels
options.why: Right: a high Km means the carrier runs well only at high lactate, as inside a hard-working fast fibre.

options.text: MCT4 binds lactate so tightly that it holds it inside the fibre
options.why: This reverses Km: a high Km means weak binding, not tight binding.

options.text: MCT1's high affinity lets it export lactate fast from fast fibres
options.why: MCT1 is mostly in oxidative fibres and mainly takes lactate in.

options.text: Affinity doesn't matter: both carry lactate equally at any level
options.why: Different Km values mean their rates depend very differently on lactate level.

variants.stem: MCTs carry an H⁺ with every lactate. What does that mean for a fast fibre during a hard effort?

options.text: Exporting lactate also exports acid, which helps protect the fibre's pH
options.why: Right: proton-linked lactate transport is part of how muscle regulates its pH.

options.text: Exporting lactate makes the fibre more acidic
options.why: The H⁺ leaves with the lactate, so export removes acid from the fibre.

options.text: MCTs need oxygen to move the H⁺
options.why: MCTs are carriers driven by concentration gradients; they use no oxygen.

options.text: The fibre takes H⁺ in while lactate goes out
options.why: Lactate and H⁺ move in the same direction, together.

variants.stem: Much of the map of where MCT1 and MCT4 sit comes from rat muscles. What is the main caution in applying it to a human cyclist?

options.text: Rat and human muscles differ in fibre mix and transporter levels, so it needs checking in humans
options.why: Right: animal data are mechanistic evidence; the human pattern must be confirmed in human biopsies (and even rat heart differs from rat muscle).

options.text: Rats don't exercise, so their muscles have no MCTs
options.why: Rat muscles have both MCTs; the issue is how well the pattern carries over to humans.

options.text: Rat studies never apply to humans, so the map should be ignored
options.why: Too strong: animal work often holds in humans; it needs confirming, not discarding.

options.text: There is none: animal data apply directly to people
options.why: Species differ; animal findings are a lower level of evidence for human claims.

variants.stem: Midway through hard 1 km intervals, a runner's blood lactate is 8 mmol·L⁻¹. What is her heart most likely doing with that lactate?

options.text: Taking it up and burning it as a main fuel
options.why: Right: the heart prefers lactate over glucose and fatty acids, and takes up more when blood lactate is high.

options.text: Keeping it out, because lactate harms heart muscle
options.why: Lactate is a preferred fuel for the heart, not a toxin.

options.text: Making more of it, because the heart is short of oxygen
options.why: The healthy heart is a net consumer of lactate, even in hard exercise.

options.text: Ignoring it, since the heart burns only fatty acids
options.why: The heart burns fatty acids, glucose and lactate; with high blood lactate, lactate's share rises.

variants.stem: In the last hard kilometres of a triathlon run, blood lactate is high. What does the brain do with it?

options.text: Takes it up and burns it, in preference to glucose
options.why: Right: in humans the brain prefers lactate over glucose as a fuel.

options.text: Nothing: lactate can't get into the brain
options.why: Lactate does cross into the brain (on MCTs) and is used there.

options.text: Stores it as brain glycogen for later
options.why: The brain burns lactate; it isn't stored as glycogen.

options.text: Releases more of it into the blood
options.why: During hard exercise the brain is a consumer of blood lactate, not a source.

variants.stem: Besides being burned, how does high blood lactate change the body's fuel use?

options.text: It turns down the use of glucose and fatty acids
options.why: Right: lactate is a preferred substrate, and high levels reduce glucose and free fatty acid use.

options.text: It speeds up fat burning in the muscle
options.why: The reverse: high lactate reduces fatty acid use.

options.text: It makes muscles take up more blood glucose
options.why: High lactate lowers glucose use; lactate is taken in its place.

options.text: It has no effect apart from being a fuel
options.why: Lactate also acts as a signal that shifts the use of other fuels.

variants.stem: A lab isolates mitochondria from human thigh muscle and finds no LDH in them and no use of lactate. What is the fairest conclusion?

options.text: It challenges the intracellular shuttle but leaves the cell–cell shuttle standing
options.why: Right: whether mitochondria use lactate directly is debated; lactate moving between cells and being burned is not.

options.text: It shows lactate is not a fuel for muscle at all
options.why: Lactate can be turned back into pyruvate in the cytosol and then oxidised; the fuel role stands.

options.text: It settles the debate in favour of the intracellular shuttle
options.why: No LDH in mitochondria is evidence against the intracellular shuttle, not for it.

options.text: It shows lactate can only be burned in the liver
options.why: Heart and slow muscle fibres burn lactate; the finding is only about where inside the cell the step happens.
